# non-pep695-generic-function (UP047)

Derived from the **pyupgrade** linter.

Fix is always available.

## What it does

Checks for use of standalone type variables and parameter specifications in generic functions.

## Why is this bad?

Special type parameter syntax was introduced in Python 3.12 by [PEP 695] for defining generic
functions. This syntax is easier to read and provides cleaner support for generics.

## Known problems

The rule currently skips generic functions nested inside of other functions or classes and those
with type parameters containing the `default` argument introduced in [PEP 696] and implemented
in Python 3.13.

Not all type checkers fully support PEP 695 yet, so even valid fixes suggested by this rule may
cause type checking to [fail].

## Fix safety

This fix is marked unsafe, as [PEP 695] uses inferred variance for type parameters, instead of
the `covariant` and `contravariant` keywords used by `TypeVar` variables. As such, replacing a
`TypeVar` variable with an inline type parameter may change its variance.

Additionally, if the rule cannot determine whether a parameter annotation corresponds to a type
variable (e.g. for a type imported from another module), it will not add the type to the generic
type parameter list. This causes the function to have a mix of old-style type variables and
new-style generic type parameters, which will be rejected by type checkers.

## Example

```python
from typing import TypeVar

T = TypeVar("T")


def generic_function(var: T) -> T:
    return var
```

Use instead:

```python
def generic_function[T](var: T) -> T:
    return var
```

## See also

This rule replaces standalone type variables in function signatures but doesn't remove
the corresponding type variables even if they are unused after the fix. See
[`unused-private-type-var`][PYI018] for a rule to clean up unused
private type variables.

This rule will not rename private type variables to remove leading underscores, even though the
new type parameters are restricted in scope to their associated function. See
[`private-type-parameter`][UP049] for a rule to update these names.

This rule only applies to generic functions and does not include generic classes. See
[`non-pep695-generic-class`][UP046] for the class version.

## Options

- `target-version`

[PEP 695]: https://peps.python.org/pep-0695/
[PEP 696]: https://peps.python.org/pep-0696/
[PYI018]: https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/unused-private-type-var/
[UP046]: https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/non-pep695-generic-class/
[UP049]: https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/private-type-parameter/
[fail]: https://github.com/python/mypy/issues/18507

analysis.fixDescription: Removes the standalone TypeVar/ParamSpec variable definitions and adds the corresponding type parameters to the function signature using PEP 695 syntax (e.g., def func[T](x: T) -> T: ...).
hazards: Rewriting changes the scope of the type variable from module-level to function-local, which can break code that references the variable outside the function (e.g., in other function signatures or class definitions).
If the TypeVar uses a 'default' argument (Python 3.13+), the fix omits the default, altering the inferred type when the parameter is omitted.
If the TypeVar has a 'bound' constraint, the fix does not preserve the bound in the new syntax, potentially changing type-checking behavior.
If the TypeVar is contravariant or covariant, the fix drops the variance keyword, and PEP 695 infers variance instead, which may differ and affect subtyping relationships.
If multiple functions share the same TypeVar, rewriting one function leaves the shared variable defined but may cause mismatches if other functions are not also rewritten.
If the TypeVar is used in a default argument value (e.g., def f(x: T = SomeDefault)), the fix does not update the default expression, leaving a reference to an undefined name after removal.
If the TypeVar is used in a type ignore comment or string annotation nearby, removing the variable definition may cause those references to become unresolved.
If the file contains a conditional import or definition of the TypeVar (e.g., inside an if block), the fix may hoist or misplace the removal, causing syntax errors.
If the TypeVar is aliased via import (e.g., from mod import TypeVar as TV), the rule may not detect it and leave the alias while incorrectly adding a type parameter, resulting in mixed old/new style.
If the function is decorated, the fix inserts type parameters before the decorator, which is invalid syntax.
If the function has overlapping type parameters with another generic function in the same scope, the fix may introduce duplicate or conflicting type parameter names.
If the code uses a stringized annotation (from __future__ import annotations) and the TypeVar is referenced in a string, removing the definition may break runtime evaluation of annotations.
